TASK: wire the feature-flag kill switches into their call sites. The flag system is built, verified and admin-manageable — but **nothing checks it**, so today it is an elaborate switch connected to nothing.

## Read first
`lib/flags.ts` (READ ONLY — do not edit). It exports `isEnabled(key, subjectId?)` and a closed `FLAGS` constant. Key properties, all proven by its author against the real database:
- 10s per-process cache; a flip takes effect within the TTL.
- Bucketing is stable per user and decorrelated across flags (`sha256("${subjectId}:${key}")`).
- Per-flag fail direction when the DB is unreachable: the four kill switches fail **CLOSED**, `feature.prompt_enhance` fails **OPEN**, `feature.sdk_engine` fails **CLOSED**.

## The exact call sites, from the flag author
| File | Where | Flag |
|---|---|---|
| `app/api/generate/route.ts` | after the project lookup, **before** the balance and spend-cap checks | `generation.enabled`, subject `user.id` |
| `app/api/projects/[id]/publish/route.ts` | after the project lookup, before the publish rate limit and moderation | `publishing.enabled` |
| `app/api/auth/signup/route.ts` | before `db.user.create` | `signups.enabled` |
| `app/api/auth/google/callback/route.ts` | before `db.user.create`, **first-time-user branch only** — an existing user signing in must be unaffected | `signups.enabled` |
| `app/api/rewards/social/claim/route.ts` | before `grantReward` | `rewards.enabled` |
| `app/api/rewards/discord/callback/route.ts` | before `grantReward` | `rewards.enabled` |
| `app/api/enhance/route.ts` | after `getCurrentUser` | `feature.prompt_enhance` |

Position matters: a killed switch must refuse **before** any spend path, any credit grant, or any model call is entered. Verify each position yourself against the current code rather than trusting the line numbers — several of these files have changed recently.

## Two things the flag author flagged for a decision
1. **`signups.enabled` and the Google callback are anonymous** — no subject id, so `isEnabled` returns false for any partial rollout. These must be operated at 100% with the switch, never a percentage. Make sure the code makes that safe and obvious.
2. **`feature.sdk_engine` is the hard one. Think before you build it.** The engine is currently selected by the `ENGINE` env var at `lib/agent.ts` (READ ONLY), and `RunOptions` carries no user id, so bucketing is impossible inside `runAgent`. The suggested site is the `runAgent(` call in the generate route. **You must reconcile it with the existing env var rather than adding a second, contradictory source of truth.** If you conclude the two cannot be reconciled cleanly without editing `lib/agent.ts` — which you may not — then DO NOT wire it: say so and explain what the right shape would be. A half-wired engine selector is worse than none.

## Response behaviour
When a switch is off, the user must get an honest, specific message — not a generic 500 and not a lie about why. Read how each route already returns errors and match it. A killed generation should not read as "you're out of credits".

## Constraints
- YOU MAY ONLY EDIT the seven route files listed above.
- DO NOT modify: prisma/schema.prisma, anything under lib/ (including flags.ts, agent.ts, credits.ts, rate-limit.ts), app/admin/**, app/projects/**, app/dashboard/**, components/**, proxy.ts, deploy.sh, .env, package.json.
- Do not change any existing behaviour other than adding the gate. Preserve the audit-logging, rate-limiting, moderation, event-tracking and credit logic already in these files exactly.
- No new npm dependencies. Do NOT run `npm run build`, `git commit`, `git push`, or `deploy.sh`.
- **HARD GATE: `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx eslint app lib components` must BOTH be clean — currently zero errors AND zero warnings.**
- Verify against the local Postgres: flip a flag off, confirm the route refuses with the right message and that nothing was written (no build row, no user, no credit grant); flip it back, confirm normal operation. Clean up every row and flag you create.

## Report back
Each site wired with its exact position and why, your decision on `feature.sdk_engine` with full reasoning, the refusal message for each, what you proved (including that a refused request writes nothing), and anything you declined to wire.

5	// Runtime feature flags and kill switches, backed by the `FeatureFlag` table.
6	//
7	// The point of this module is that a behaviour change does NOT require a
8	// deploy. `deploy.sh` on this project has a history of shipping stale code,
9	// and a kill switch that needs a deploy is not a kill switch — it is a
10	// postmortem action item. Flipping a row here takes effect everywhere within
11	// one cache TTL (see FLAG_CACHE_TTL_MS below), with no build, no restart and
12	// no risk of shipping whatever else happened to be sitting on main.
13	//
14	// Three rules keep it honest, and they are the same three that keep
15	// lib/events.ts useful:
16	//
17	// 1. KEYS ARE A CLOSED SET. FLAGS below is the whole vocabulary. Free-text
18	//    flag keys rot exactly like free-text event names: someone checks
19	//    "publish_enabled" while the admin page writes "publishing.enabled", the
20	//    check silently reads a missing row forever, and the kill switch that
21	//    everyone believes exists does nothing on the day it matters.
22	// 2. EVERY FLAG READS AS A CAPABILITY THAT IS ON. `generation.enabled` is
23	//    true when generation works. There is no flag whose `enabled = true` means
24	//    "the thing is broken/off" — inverted flags are how someone turns
25	//    generation OFF at 3am while trying to turn it off.
26	// 3. BEHAVIOUR WHEN THE DATABASE IS NOT THERE IS DECLARED PER FLAG, in code,
27	//    next to the flag. See `whenUnavailable`.
28

170	// ── Caching ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
171	//
172	// A database round trip per flag check per request is not acceptable —
173	// /api/generate alone would want three of them before it does any work. A
174	// stale cache is not acceptable either, because a kill switch is only as good
175	// as the delay between the click and the effect.
176	//
177	// 10 seconds is the compromise, and the number is chosen from both ends:
178	//
179	//   Freshness. An incident responder clicks "Turn off", waits out one TTL and
180	//   the whole fleet has converged. Ten seconds is shorter than the time it
181	//   takes to alt-tab to the dashboard and confirm the graph moved, so the
182	//   switch feels immediate rather than broken. A minute does not: at a minute
183	//   people click it twice, then start looking for a deploy button, which is
184	//   the exact failure mode this module exists to remove.
185	//
186	//   Cost. The refresh reads the WHOLE TABLE in one query, not one query per
187	//   key, so the cost is 1 query / 10s / process regardless of how many flags
188	//   exist or how many are checked per request. That is ~0.1 qps per process —
189	//   noise next to any real request. Dropping to 1s would buy nine seconds of
190	//   freshness nobody can act on, for 10x the queries.
191	//
192	// The cache is PER PROCESS and deliberately not shared. There is no Redis
193	// here, and adding one to hold six booleans would be its own outage surface.
194	// The consequence is worth stating plainly: a multi-process or multi-instance
195	// deploy does not flip atomically, it CONVERGES within one TTL. Every process
196	// independently notices within 10s. `invalidateFlagCache()` shortcuts this,
197	// but only for the process that ran the write — which in practice is the one
198	// serving the admin page, so the admin sees their own change immediately and
199	// everyone else sees it within the TTL.
200	export const FLAG_CACHE_TTL_MS = 10_000;
201	
202	/**
203	 * After a failed read, wait this long before hammering a database that is
204	 * already unhappy. Short enough that recovery is fast, long enough that a hot
205	 * path does not turn one outage into a connection storm.
206	 */
207	const ERROR_BACKOFF_MS = 2_000;
208	
209	type FlagState = { enabled: boolean; rolloutPct: number };
210	
211	let cache: { rows: Map<string, FlagState>; loadedAt: number } | null = null;
212	let nextAttemptAt = 0;
213	let inFlight: Promise<Map<string, FlagState> | null> | null = null;
214	/**
215	 * Bumped by every `invalidateFlagCache()`. A read carries the epoch it started
216	 * under and refuses to publish its result if that epoch is stale — see the note
217	 * in `refresh()`. Without this, invalidation is not actually a guarantee.
218	 */
219	let epoch = 0;
220	
221	async function refresh(): Promise<Map<string, FlagState> | null> {
222	  const startedAt = epoch;
223	  try {
224	    const rows = await db.featureFlag.findMany({
225	      select: { key: true, enabled: true, rolloutPct: true },
226	    });
227	    const map = new Map<string, FlagState>(
228	      rows.map((r) => [r.key, { enabled: r.enabled, rolloutPct: r.rolloutPct }]),
229	    );
230	    // If the cache was invalidated while this query was in flight, the query
231	    // began before the write that invalidated it and therefore cannot have seen
232	    // it. Caching this result would resurrect the pre-write value for a full
233	    // TTL — in the very process that performed the write, which is the one
234	    // process this module promises will see its own change immediately. The
235	    // callers already awaiting this promise still get the rows (their read
236	    // genuinely predates the write); the next caller starts a fresh query.
237	    if (startedAt === epoch) {
238	      cache = { rows: map, loadedAt: Date.now() };
239	      nextAttemptAt = 0;
240	    }
241	    return map;
242	  } catch (err) {
243	    console.error("[flags] failed to read FeatureFlag; serving last known values", err);
244	    if (startedAt === epoch) nextAttemptAt = Date.now() + ERROR_BACKOFF_MS;
245	    // Stale-if-error. A snapshot from an hour ago still carries the operator's
246	    // last intent, which is a far better answer than the hardcoded default —
247	    // and it is what makes failing closed on kill switches cheap: a switch you
248	    // turned off stays off through the outage instead of springing back open.
249	    return cache?.rows ?? null;
250	  } finally {
251	    // Only if it is still ours: an invalidation already cleared the slot and a
252	    // newer read may have claimed it.
253	    if (startedAt === epoch) inFlight = null;
254	  }
255	}

257	/** Null only when the table has never been read successfully by this process. */
258	async function snapshot(): Promise<Map<string, FlagState> | null> {
259	  const now = Date.now();
260	  if (cache && now - cache.loadedAt < FLAG_CACHE_TTL_MS) return cache.rows;
261	  if (now < nextAttemptAt) return cache?.rows ?? null;
262	  // Single-flight: on a busy process the TTL expires for many concurrent
263	  // requests at once, and they must share one query rather than each opening
264	  // their own.
265	  inFlight ??= refresh();
266	  return inFlight;
267	}

269	/**
270	 * Drop this process's cached snapshot. Other processes converge within
271	 * FLAG_CACHE_TTL_MS.
272	 *
273	 * Called after every write, so it must also disown any read that is currently
274	 * in flight — that read was issued before the write committed, so joining it
275	 * (or letting it populate the cache when it lands) would serve the pre-write
276	 * value. Bumping the epoch does both.
277	 */
278	export function invalidateFlagCache(): void {
279	  cache = null;
280	  nextAttemptAt = 0;
281	  inFlight = null;
282	  epoch++;
283	}

285	// ── Rollout bucketing ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
286	//
287	// `rolloutPct` needs a bucket per subject, and the two obvious cheap options
288	// are both wrong:
289	//
290	//   Math.random() < pct  — the same user gets a different answer on every
291	//   request. A 50% rollout of a UI feature makes it flicker between page
292	//   loads, a 50% rollout of an engine splits ONE user's builds across both
293	//   engines, and any comparison between the two arms is contaminated because
294	//   nobody is durably in either.
295	//
296	//   A cheap function of the id alone (id.charCodeAt, id.length % 100) — cuids
297	//   share a timestamp-derived prefix, so ids created near each other land in
298	//   the same bucket and 10% selects a contiguous block of one afternoon's
299	//   signups rather than a random tenth of the user base.
300	//
301	// So: sha256 over `${subjectId}:${key}`, first 4 bytes as a uint32, mod 100.
302	//
303	//   Hashing the SUBJECT makes the answer stable — same user, same flag, same
304	//   answer on every request, in every process, across restarts and deploys,
305	//   with no state stored anywhere.
306	//
307	//   Mixing in the KEY decorrelates flags. Hash the user id alone and every
308	//   flag set to 50% picks the *same* half of the user base: the unluckiest
309	//   users get every experiment at once, and two independent 50% rollouts are
310	//   silently a single cohort. With the key mixed in, each flag gets its own
311	//   independent shuffle.
312	//
313	//   sha256 comes from node:crypto (no dependency) and avalanches properly, so
314	//   the buckets are uniform. It costs roughly a microsecond on a ~40 byte
315	//   input — irrelevant, since it replaces a database round trip, not a
316	//   comparison. Modulo bias over a uint32 into 100 buckets is on the order of
317	//   1e-8 and does not matter at any user count this product will ever see.
318	export function rolloutBucket(subjectId: string, key: string): number {
319	  return createHash("sha256").update(`${subjectId}:${key}`).digest().readUInt32BE(0) % 100;
320	}

322	/**
323	 * Is this flag on, for this subject, right now?
324	 *
325	 * `userId` is the bucketing subject for partial rollouts. Any stable
326	 * identifier works (a user id is the right one; a project owner's id would
327	 * do), but it must be stable for that subject or the rollout stops being a
328	 * rollout — see `rolloutBucket`.
329	 *
330	 * Resolution order, and why each step is where it is:
331	 *   1. Database unreadable and nothing ever cached → the flag's declared
332	 *      `whenUnavailable`. Per flag, on purpose.
333	 *   2. No row for the key → the flag's declared `whenUnset`. A missing row is
334	 *      a fresh environment, not an incident.
335	 *   3. `enabled === false` → false. Matches the schema's own note that
336	 *      `rolloutPct` is ignored when `enabled` is false: "off" means off, and a
337	 *      leftover 100 in the percentage column must never resurrect it.
338	 *   4. Otherwise bucket by `rolloutPct`.
339	 */
340	export async function isEnabled(key: FlagKey, userId?: string | null): Promise<boolean> {
341	  const spec = FLAG_SPECS[key];
342	  const rows = await snapshot();
343	  if (rows === null) return spec.whenUnavailable;
344	
345	  const row = rows.get(key);
346	  if (!row) return spec.whenUnset;
347	  if (!row.enabled) return false;
348	  if (row.rolloutPct >= 100) return true;
349	  if (row.rolloutPct <= 0) return false;
350	
351	  // No subject means no stable bucket, and pretending otherwise would put the
352	  // same anonymous visitor on both sides of the split across two requests.
353	  // Resolving to false is the safe direction in both cases: a partially-shed
354	  // kill switch sheds MORE (over-killing beats under-killing in an incident),
355	  // and an anonymous visitor simply does not get a half-rolled-out feature.
356	  // Note the operational consequence: a kill switch left at rolloutPct < 100
357	  // is effectively fully off for signups, which are anonymous by definition.
358	  // Kill switches are meant to be operated at 100 and toggled with `enabled`.
359	  if (!userId) return false;
360	
361	  return rolloutBucket(userId, key) < row.rolloutPct;
362	}

All six flags wired across the seven sites, both gates clean, and every test row removed.

## What was wired

| Site | Exact position | Flag / subject | Refusal |
|---|---|---|---|
| `app/api/generate/route.ts:62` | After the project lookup/404, **before** `getBalance` | `generation.enabled`, `user.id` | 503 — "Building is paused right now while we sort out a problem on our side. Nothing has been charged and your project is untouched — please try again in a few minutes." |
| `app/api/projects/[id]/publish/route.ts:57` | After the project 404, **before** the empty-files 400, the rate limit, the secret scan, moderation and the publish transaction | `publishing.enabled`, `user.id` | 503 — "Publishing is paused right now while we work through an issue. Your site is saved and nothing has changed — try publishing again shortly." |
| `app/api/auth/signup/route.ts:48` | After the two shape 400s, **before** `checkSignupRateLimit`, the existence check and `db.user.create` | `signups.enabled`, **no subject** | 503 — "New sign-ups are paused right now. No account was created — please try again a little later." |
| `app/api/auth/google/callback/route.ts:109` | Inside the `else` of `if (existing)`, inside `if (!user)` — the new-account branch only, before `db.user.create` | `signups.enabled`, **no subject** | 302 → `/login?error=signups_paused` |
| `app/api/rewards/social/claim/route.ts:74` | Immediately before `grantReward` | `rewards.enabled`, `user.id` | 503 — "Reward claims are paused right now. Nothing has been credited and your connected account is still saved — try claiming again later." |
| `app/api/rewards/discord/callback/route.ts:165` | Immediately before `grantReward` | `rewards.enabled`, `user.id` | 302 → `/settings?reward=unavailable` → "That reward isn't available right now." |
| `app/api/enhance/route.ts:41` | Immediately after `getCurrentUser`, before the body checks, the rate limiter and `enhancePrompt` | `feature.prompt_enhance`, `user.id` | 503 — "Enhance is switched off right now — you can still build with what you wrote." |

**Positions I chose deliberately, against the current code:**
- **Generate:** the two checks immediately below both answer 402 and both talk about credits. The kill switch gets its own 503 and its own words so a killed build never reads as "you're out of credits" — proven below.
- **Signup:** ahead of the existence check, not just ahead of `db.user.create`. That 409 is the only response on the route that differs for a registered address; a route that cannot mint an account has no business still answering the enumeration oracle. Also ahead of the rate limiter, which `record()`s a hit per attempt.
- **Publish:** ahead of the empty-files 400. During an incident the switch is the more useful truth.
- **Subjects:** I passed `user.id` at every site where a signed-in user exists, not only at generate. The spec table names a subject only for generate, but `isEnabled` resolves any `rolloutPct < 100` to **false** without one — so omitting an available subject turns a partial percentage into a full shed. At 100%/`enabled` (how kill switches are meant to be run) it changes nothing.

## `feature.sdk_engine` — NOT wired, deliberately

It cannot be wired from the generate route without editing `lib/agent.ts`, which is off-limits. Every route-side option is a dead end:

1. **Pass it through `runAgent`** — `RunOptions` has no engine field; TypeScript rejects the excess property and `runAgent` would ignore it. The engine is chosen by the module-level `export const ENGINE = process.env.KODELY_ENGINE === "sdk" ? "sdk" : "api"`, read once at module load, entirely inside `runAgent`.
2. **Call `runAgentSdk` directly from the route** — its signature is `runAgentSdk(opts, SYSTEM)`, and `SYSTEM` is a module-private `const` in `lib/agent.ts`. Duplicating a ~100-line prompt into the route is not a workaround: `lib/agent-sdk.ts` rewrites that prompt by **exact string replacement** (`API_TOOL_CONTRACT`, `API_ASSET_CONTRACT`). A copy that drifts by one character silently stops swapping the tool contract, and the file's own comment records that this exact failure already shipped to prod once — the agent announced it was building, reached for `write_file`, and wrote nothing.
3. **Mutate `process.env.KODELY_ENGINE` per request** — `ENGINE` is already evaluated, so it wouldn't take effect; and a process-global write would flip the engine under other in-flight builds.

So the flag can be *read* in the route but the decision cannot be *delivered*. A gate that reads a flag and then does nothing with it is exactly the "elaborate switch connected to nothing" this task exists to remove, so I left it unwired rather than half-wired.

**The right shape** (one small edit to `lib/agent.ts`, which keeps a single source of truth rather than adding a second):

```ts
// RunOptions
/** Overrides the ENGINE default for this run. */
engine?: "api" | "sdk";

// runAgent
const engine = ENGINE === "sdk" ? "sdk" : (opts.engine ?? "api");
if (engine === "sdk") { ... }
```

`runAgent` stays the only place that decides. `KODELY_ENGINE=sdk` remains an absolute pin — it is an operator's deliberate machine-level choice to stay off the metered key, and a flag whose `whenUnset` is `false` must never silently revoke it (that inversion is the contradictory-second-source trap). When the env var is at its `api` default, the flag becomes the rollout dial, and the route passes `engine: (await isEnabled(FLAGS.sdkEngine, user.id)) ? "sdk" : "api"`. This is a strict extension: both current env values behave exactly as today, and `api` machines gain a stable per-user bucket onto the SDK. Bucketing on `user.id` (not per build) also matters here — `rolloutBucket` is what stops one user's builds from being split across both engines, which would contaminate any comparison between the two arms.

## What I proved against the local Postgres

Baseline `FeatureFlag` was empty; counts were users 4 / projects 10 / builds 10 / ledger 6 / files 141 / messages 16 / sessions 2. I seeded a test user, session, project and build file directly, then flipped each flag off and on with a >10s wait for the cache TTL.

- **generation** — off: 503 with the paused message; project had **0 build rows and 0 message rows** afterwards, globally unchanged. On: real request returned `200 text/event-stream` and streamed `{"type":"status","text":"Building your site…"}` with a build row written. **Message distinctness proven directly:** with balance drained to 0 and the flag *on* → `402 "You're out of credits."`; same zero balance with the flag *off* → the 503 paused message. The kill switch wins and never reads as a billing problem.
- **publishing** — off: 503; `publishedAt` still `null`, 0 published files. On: `200 {"url":"https://…kodely.site"}`, `publishedAt` set, 1 published file.
- **signups** — the dev server's rate limiter happens to be stuck at its cold-start fail-closed 429 (pre-existing, in `lib/rate-limit.ts`, unrelated to this change), which gave a clean ordering proof: flag off → my 503; flag on → 429 from the limiter, i.e. the gate falls through and existing behaviour is untouched. Malformed body still answered `400 "Enter a valid email."` in both states. **User count never moved.** I also reproduced the trap from note #1: `enabled=true, rolloutPct=50` → anonymous → **fully refused**; back at 100 → falls through normally.
- **rewards** — the two reward routes short-circuit on this box because no reward env vars are set, so I stood up a throwaway copy of the app on port 3578 with `KODELY_INSTAGRAM_URL` and a test salt (the real `.env` was never touched), planted a matured pending claim, and: off → 503, pending row untouched, **ledger count 17 → 17, no credits granted**; on → `200 {"state":"claimed","credits":50}` with the `reward:instagram:…` ledger row written.
- **prompt_enhance** — unset → real spec returned; off → 503 with the honest message; `rolloutPct=0` → off; back to 100 → real spec returned. `401 "Not signed in."` still answers first, confirming the gate sits after auth.
- **Final all-clear** with the flag table empty again: all seven routes return their normal pre-existing answers.

**Not proven by execution, only by inspection** (I want to be explicit): the **Discord callback** gate and the **Google callback** gate cannot be reached over HTTP without a real third-party OAuth round trip. Both are a single `if` immediately before the sole side-effecting call, using the helper proven at five other sites. For Discord I did confirm the exact redirect shape my gate emits is already live and mapped — the no-config path produced `302 → /settings?reward=unavailable`. I also did not re-prove the DB-unreachable fail directions; that is the flag author's verified behaviour and re-testing it meant taking Postgres down under a concurrent tester.

## One follow-up you'll want (outside my allowlist)
